period_summary: Citations of Proverbs 8:22 are concentrated in the 4th century during the Arian controversy, where the verse became the central proof-text debated between Arians and Nicenes. Earlier 2nd–3rd century citations (Justin, Irenaeus, Origen) establish the verse's christological reading prior to its weaponization in the Trinitarian disputes.

citations.cited_text: κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Justin uses ἔκτισέ ('created'), the standard LXX rendering of Hebrew קנני, rather than ἐκτήσατο ('possessed/acquired') found in Aquila and closer to MT. The wording matches the Old Greek tradition exactly.
citations.theological_use: Justin cites the verse to prove that Christ as Wisdom/Logos was generated by the Father before all creatures, distinct from yet originating from him. He uses it apologetically against Trypho to show pre-existent divine plurality.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms ἔκτισέ as the established Greek reading by the mid-2nd century in Rome, prior to any controversy over the verb.

citations.cited_text: Dominus creavit me principium viarum suarum in opera sua
citations.text_form_note: The Latin 'creavit' translates ἔκτισέ, reflecting the LXX. The Old Latin tradition Irenaeus uses follows the Greek faithfully.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus identifies Wisdom with the Spirit (or in some passages the Son) as eternally with the Father, using the verse to support the existence of God's Wisdom before creation.
citations.transmission_implication: Demonstrates that the LXX form was already mediated into Latin and circulating in Western Christianity by the late 2nd century.

citations.cited_text: κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Origen explicitly cites the LXX wording. In the Hexapla he would have known of Aquila's ἐκτήσατο, but for theological exegesis he uses the Old Greek ἔκτισέ.
citations.theological_use: Origen identifies Wisdom as the Son/Logos and reads 'created' as referring to the Son's eternal generation as the beginning (ἀρχή) of God's ways, foundational to his Logos Christology.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's awareness of variant Greek versions shows the verse was already a site of textual-theological attention before Nicaea.

citations.cited_text: κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius accepts the LXX text including ἔκτισέ as authoritative; he does not dispute the wording but reinterprets it. He is aware that Aquila and Symmachus read ἐκτήσατο but does not appeal to them to evade the Arian argument.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius devotes nearly two-thirds of Oration 2 to this verse, arguing that 'created' refers to the Incarnation (the assumed humanity), not the eternal generation of the Son, thereby refuting Arian subordinationism.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms the LXX reading as the standard 4th-century ecclesiastical text even when theologically inconvenient.

citations.cited_text: κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius cites the standard LXX form with ἔκτισέ. Given his Hexaplaric expertise, he would have known the alternatives but uses the Old Greek.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius reads the verse as referring to the Son's pre-temporal generation as the beginning of God's economy, in a subordinationist key consistent with his anti-Marcellan stance.
citations.transmission_implication: Caesarean text-form evidence aligns with the broader LXX tradition.

citations.cited_text: κύριος ἔκτισέν με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ
citations.text_form_note: Basil cites the LXX ἔκτισέ but explicitly notes that other translators (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) read ἐκτήσατο, and appeals to this Hebrew-aligned alternative as theologically preferable. His argumentative use draws on multiple text forms.
citations.theological_use: Basil argues against Eunomius that 'created' need not imply ontological inferiority, supplementing with the variant ἐκτήσατο ('acquired/possessed') to weaken the Arian reading.
citations.transmission_implication: Reveals the conscious 4th-century pro-Nicene strategy of invoking Hexaplaric variants to counter Arian exegesis of the Septuagint.

citations.cited_text: Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum
citations.text_form_note: Jerome's Vulgate translates the Hebrew קנני as 'possedit' ('possessed'), aligning with Aquila's ἐκτήσατο and the proto-MT against the LXX ἔκτισέ.
citations.theological_use: Jerome uses the Hebrew-based reading to neutralize the Arian proof-text, since 'possessed' implies eternal coexistence rather than creation.
citations.transmission_implication: Marks the decisive Western shift toward the Hebrew text-form in the Latin tradition, with explicit anti-Arian theological motivation.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citations reveal that the LXX reading κύριος ἔκτισέν με ('the Lord created me') was the dominant and effectively uniform text form in Greek-speaking Christianity from the 2nd through the 4th centuries, mediated into Latin as 'creavit me' through the Old Latin. Awareness of the alternative ἐκτήσατο ('possessed') from Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion existed at least from Origen's Hexapla onward, but it was theologically activated only during the Arian controversy. The Cappadocians (Basil) selectively invoked the Hebrew-aligned variant as a polemical tool, while Athanasius held the line on the LXX wording but reinterpreted its referent. Jerome's Vulgate 'possedit' represents a definitive late-4th-century Latin pivot toward the Hebraica veritas, driven by the same anti-Arian pressures that shaped Greek exegesis.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christians overwhelmingly read this verse as 'The Lord created me' from the Greek Old Testament, and this remained the standard wording for centuries. When Arians used it to argue Christ was a creature, theologians like Athanasius reinterpreted what 'created' meant, while Jerome eventually translated directly from Hebrew as 'possessed me,' which fit Nicene theology better and shaped the later Latin Bible.

notable_variants.significance: The dominant patristic reading, reflecting the Old Greek translation of Hebrew קנני. Its persistence through the Arian controversy demonstrates the LXX's authoritative status even when theologically problematic.

Reflects the Hebrew root קנה in its 'acquire/possess' sense, attested in Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and adopted by the Vulgate. Its rise in patristic citation marks the recovery of proto-MT readings under theological pressure.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Arian Controversy Forces Hebraic Textual Recovery
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: Proverbs 8:22 is the paradigmatic case of doctrinal controversy driving textual revision: the LXX ἔκτισέ was uncontested for two centuries until Arian exegesis weaponized it, prompting pro-Nicene fathers to reach for Hexaplaric Hebrew-aligned alternatives. Jerome's choice of 'possedit' in the Vulgate institutionalizes this shift, demonstrating that the Latin West's turn to the Hebraica veritas was not purely philological but theologically catalyzed.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: This single verse shows how a major theological dispute pushed Christians to look back at the Hebrew Bible rather than rely solely on the Greek translation, permanently changing how the verse was read in the West.
